PR 6: Opening the Transformer¶

Attention, Encoder, Decoder and Inference with Pretrained Models¶

0. Libraries, Seeds & Model IDs¶

In [1]:

  • All libraries were imported and the random seed (42) was set for reproducible results.

Task 1: Introduction, History, Pipelines & Tokenizer¶

1.1 Install and First Pipeline¶

In [2]:
clf = pipeline("sentiment-analysis", model=DISTIL_SST2)

sentences = [
    "I absolutely loved this movie, the acting was brilliant!",   # positive
    "The food was cold and the service was terrible.",            # negative
    "The hotel room was okay, nothing special.",                  # neutral-ish
    "The film was not bad at all.",                               # tricky: negation
    "I wanted to like this book, but I could not finish it.",     # tricky: mixed
]

results = clf(sentences)

pipe_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Sentence": sentences,
    "Label": [r["label"] for r in results],
    "Score": [round(r["score"], 4) for r in results],
})
display(pipe_df)

Sentence Label Score
0 I absolutely loved this movie, the acting was ... POSITIVE 0.9999
1 The food was cold and the service was terrible. NEGATIVE 0.9997

3 The film was not bad at all. POSITIVE 0.9975

  • One pipeline() call hides three steps: (1) tokenisation (text → ids), (2) model forward pass (ids → logits), (3) post-processing (softmax → label + score).
  • The model only knows two labels: POSITIVE and NEGATIVE, so a neutral sentence is forced into one of them.
  • The negation sentence ("not bad at all") is the real test — check whether the model understood it.

1.2 Introduction & History of Transformers¶

Year Model / Paper Why it mattered
2014 Seq2Seq with attention (Bahdanau et al.) Decoder could look back at all encoder states instead of one fixed vector
2015 Luong attention (Luong et al.) Simpler dot / general attention scores for translation
2017 "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al.) Removed RNNs completely — only attention; fully parallel training
2018 BERT (Devlin et al.) and GPT (Radford et al.) Pre-train a big Transformer once, fine-tune for many tasks
2019 GPT-2, T5, DistilBERT Bigger text generators, text-to-text framework, and a smaller faster BERT
2020 GPT-3, Vision Transformer (ViT) Huge language models; Transformers also work on image patches
2022+ Chat assistants and other large language models Transformers became everyday tools

What problem with RNNs / LSTMs did the Transformer solve?

  • RNNs read a sentence one word at a time, so they are sequential and cannot use the GPU in parallel → slow training.
  • LSTMs have short memory: information from early words fades by the time the sentence ends.
  • Attention lets every word look directly at every other word, so long-range links are easy and the whole sequence is processed in parallel.

1.3 Impact & Disadvantages¶

Impact (what Transformers changed):

  • Translation — fast and fluent machine translation.
  • Search — better understanding of search queries and documents.
  • Chat assistants — ChatGPT-style conversation and question answering.
  • Code completion — suggesting and writing code.
  • Image models — Vision Transformers for classification and detection.
  • Protein structure — attention-based models help predict how proteins fold.

Disadvantages (we measure two of them in Task 6):

  • Quadratic attention cost — compute and memory grow with the square of the sequence length. (measured in 6.3)
  • Fixed context window — text beyond the limit (512 tokens here) is lost. (measured in 6.2)
  • Large compute and memory needs for training and running big models.
  • Need for huge data to pre-train well.
  • Hallucination in generative models — fluent but false answers. (measured in 6.4)
  • Opaque behaviour — hard to explain why a model gave an answer.

1.4 Tokenizer in Action¶

In [3]:
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(DISTIL_SST2)

text = "Transformers are surprisingly easy to understand."
enc = tok(text)

print("Tokens         :", tok.tokenize(text))
print("input_ids      :", enc["input_ids"])
print("attention_mask :", enc["attention_mask"])
print("With specials  :", tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(enc["input_ids"]))
print("Special tokens : CLS =", tok.cls_token, "| SEP =", tok.sep_token, "| PAD =", tok.pad_token)

# A rare / long word is split into sub-word pieces ('##' means 'continues the previous piece')
rare_word = "Antidisestablishmentarianism"
pieces = tok.tokenize(rare_word)
print("\nRare word      :", rare_word)
print("Sub-word pieces:", pieces, f"({len(pieces)} pieces)")

Tokens         : ['transformers', 'are', 'surprisingly', 'easy', 'to', 'understand', '.']
input_ids      : [101, 19081, 2024, 10889, 3733, 2000, 3305, 1012, 102]
attention_mask : [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
With specials  : ['[CLS]', 'transformers', 'are', 'surprisingly', 'easy', 'to', 'understand', '.', '[SEP]']
Special tokens : CLS = [CLS] | SEP = [SEP] | PAD = [PAD]

Rare word      : Antidisestablishmentarianism
Sub-word pieces: ['anti', '##dis', '##est', '##ab', '##lish', '##ment', '##arian', '##ism'] (8 pieces)
  • The tokenizer adds [CLS] at the start and [SEP] at the end. [CLS] collects a summary of the whole sentence (used for classification) and [SEP] marks the end of a sentence.
  • Words are converted to integer ids because the model can only work with numbers.
  • Rare words are broken into sub-word pieces (## pieces). This keeps the vocabulary small (about 30k) but still lets the model handle any word, even one it never saw.

  • Sentences in a batch must have the same length, so the shorter one is filled with [PAD] tokens (id 0).
  • attention_mask = 1 for real tokens and 0 for padding, so the model ignores padding. We prove this in Task 4.8.

Task 2: Self-Attention & Scaled Dot-Product Attention¶

2.1 Self-Attention Idea¶

Every token is turned into three vectors:

  • Query (Q) — what am I looking for?
  • Key (K) — what do I offer?
  • Value (V) — what do I pass on?

A token's new representation is a weighted average of all Value vectors. The weights come from how well its Query matches every Key (high match → high weight). Because all tokens are handled together as matrices, the whole sequence is processed in parallel, unlike an RNN.

$$\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

2.2 Scaled Dot-Product Attention from Scratch¶

In [6]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    x = x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)      # subtract max -> numerically stable
    e = np.exp(x)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    d_k = Q.shape[-1]
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)              # (tokens x tokens)
    if mask is not None:
        scores = scores + mask                   # used later for causal masking
    weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)           # every row sums to 1
    output = weights @ V                         # weighted average of Values
    return output, weights, scores

# 4 tokens, d_model = 8
words = ["The", "cat", "sat", "down"]
d_model = 8
X  = rng.normal(size=(4, d_model))
Wq = rng.normal(size=(d_model, d_model))
Wk = rng.normal(size=(d_model, d_model))
Wv = rng.normal(size=(d_model, d_model))

def self_attention(X):
    Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
    return scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V)

Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
output, weights, scores = scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V)

print("X:", X.shape, "| Q:", Q.shape, "| K:", K.shape, "| V:", V.shape)
print("scores:", scores.shape, "| weights:", weights.shape, "| output:", output.shape)
print("Row sums of weights:", weights.sum(axis=1).round(6))
print("All rows sum to 1 ?", np.allclose(weights.sum(axis=1), 1))

plt.figure(figsize=(5, 4))
sns.heatmap(weights, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="viridis", xticklabels=words, yticklabels=words)
plt.title("Attention Weights from Scratch (4x4)")
plt.xlabel("Key (attended token)")
plt.ylabel("Query (current token)")
save_fig("attention_scratch.png")
plt.show()

X: (4, 8) | Q: (4, 8) | K: (4, 8) | V: (4, 8)
scores: (4, 4) | weights: (4, 4) | output: (4, 8)
Row sums of weights: [1. 1. 1. 1.]
All rows sum to 1 ? True
  • Q, K, V are made by multiplying the input X with three learned matrices.
  • The 4×4 weights matrix shows how much each token (row) attends to every other token (column).
  • Every row sums to 1 (softmax), so each output is a proper weighted average of the Value vectors.

2.3 Why Divide by √d_k?¶

In [7]:
def entropy(w):
    return -(w * np.log(w + 1e-12)).sum(axis=-1)

rows = []
for d_k in [4, 256]:
    Qr = rng.normal(size=(8, d_k))
    Kr = rng.normal(size=(8, d_k))
    for scaled in [False, True]:
        s = Qr @ Kr.T
        if scaled:
            s = s / np.sqrt(d_k)
        w = softmax(s)
        rows.append({
            "d_k": d_k,
            "Scaling": "WITH 1/sqrt(d_k)" if scaled else "WITHOUT",
            "Score std": round(s.std(), 2),
            "Avg max softmax prob": round(w.max(axis=-1).mean(), 3),
            "Avg entropy": round(entropy(w).mean(), 3),
        })

scaling_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
display(scaling_df)
print("Maximum possible entropy for 8 tokens = ln(8) =", round(np.log(8), 3))
d_k Scaling Score std Avg max softmax prob Avg entropy
0 4 WITHOUT 1.83 0.587 1.196
1 4 WITH 1/sqrt(d_k) 0.92 0.359 1.750
2 256 WITHOUT 15.77 0.859 0.290
3 256 WITH 1/sqrt(d_k) 0.99 0.362 1.707 
Maximum possible entropy for 8 tokens = ln(8) = 2.079
  • A dot product of two random vectors has variance d_k, so scores get larger as d_k grows (see the Score std column).
  • Without scaling and with a large d_k, softmax is pushed into a saturated region: one weight is almost 1 and the rest almost 0 (max prob → 1, entropy → 0). There the gradients almost vanish, so learning stops.
  • Dividing by √d_k keeps the score variance near 1, so the attention stays soft and trainable for any d_k.

2.4 Self-Attention vs Luong Attention¶

In [8]:
def luong_dot_attention(encoder_states, decoder_state):
    scores = encoder_states @ decoder_state          # one score per encoder state
    weights = softmax(scores)
    context = weights @ encoder_states               # weighted sum of encoder states
    return weights, context

encoder_states = rng.normal(size=(5, 8))             # 5 source positions
decoder_state  = rng.normal(size=(8,))               # 1 decoder hidden state

luong_weights, luong_context = luong_dot_attention(encoder_states, decoder_state)
print("Luong weights :", luong_weights.round(3), "| sum =", luong_weights.sum().round(3))
print("Context vector shape:", luong_context.shape)

Luong weights : [0.    0.732 0.    0.265 0.003] | sum = 1.0
Context vector shape: (8,)
Feature Luong (dot) attention Self-attention
Where Q, K, V come from Q = decoder state; K = V = encoder states Q, K, V all come from the same sequence (via W_q, W_k, W_v)
What is attended over Decoder state looks at encoder states Every token looks at every token
Needs an RNN? Yes (encoder and decoder are RNNs) No
Parallelism Sequential (RNN steps) Fully parallel
Where in architecture Between RNN decoder and RNN encoder Inside every Transformer layer

2.5 Attention Is Order-Blind¶

In [9]:
perm = np.array([2, 0, 3, 1])                  # fixed shuffle of the 4 rows

out_original, _, _ = self_attention(X)
out_shuffled, _, _ = self_attention(X[perm])

print("Shuffled-input output == original output re-permuted ?", np.allclose(out_shuffled, out_original[perm]))
print("Shuffled-input output == original output (no re-permute)?", np.allclose(out_shuffled, out_original))

Shuffled-input output == original output re-permuted ? True
Shuffled-input output == original output (no re-permute)? False
  • After shuffling the input rows, the output rows are the same rows, only in shuffled order (True above).
  • So self-attention has no idea of word order — "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look the same. This is exactly why positional encoding is needed (Task 3).

2.6 Verify Against a Real Model (DistilBERT Layer 0, Head 0)¶

In [10]:
sentence = "The animal did not cross the street because it was too tired."
enc = tok(sentence, return_tensors="pt")

with torch.no_grad():
    out = distil(**enc, output_hidden_states=True, output_attentions=True)

# Layer-0 attention module (look at the names: q_lin, k_lin, v_lin, out_lin)
layer0_attn = distil.distilbert.transformer.layer[0].attention
print(layer0_attn)

x = out.hidden_states[0]                               # input of layer 0: (1, tokens, 768)
n_heads, d_head = 12, 64

with torch.no_grad():
    q = layer0_attn.q_lin(x)
    k = layer0_attn.k_lin(x)

B, T, _ = q.shape
q = q.view(B, T, n_heads, d_head).transpose(1, 2)      # (1, 12, T, 64)
k = k.view(B, T, n_heads, d_head).transpose(1, 2)

my_scores  = q @ k.transpose(-1, -2) / np.sqrt(d_head)  # no padding in one sentence -> no mask needed
my_weights = torch.softmax(my_scores, dim=-1)

real_weights = out.attentions[0][0, 0]                 # layer 0, head 0 -> (T, T)
mine = my_weights[0, 0]

max_diff = (mine - real_weights).abs().max().item()
print("\nMaximum absolute difference:", max_diff)
print("np.allclose (tolerance 1e-4):", np.allclose(mine.numpy(), real_weights.numpy(), atol=1e-4))

MultiHeadSelfAttention(
  (dropout): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
  (q_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
  (k_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
  (v_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
  (out_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
)

Maximum absolute difference: 0.0
np.allclose (tolerance 1e-4): True
  • We took the real hidden states, applied the layer's own q_lin and k_lin, split into 12 heads of size 64, and applied softmax(QKᵀ/√64).
  • A tiny maximum difference (≈ 1e-7) and True from np.allclose prove that our NumPy-style attention is exactly what the real Transformer computes — nothing is hidden or magic.

Task 3: Multi-Head Attention, Positional Encoding & Layer Normalization¶

3.1 Multi-Head Attention¶

One attention pattern is not enough: a word may need to look at its neighbour for grammar, at a noun for meaning and at a punctuation mark for structure — all at the same time.

  • With h heads, d_model is split into h smaller subspaces (DistilBERT: 768 = 12 × 64).
  • Each head has its own Q, K, V projections and learns its own attention pattern.
  • The heads' outputs are concatenated and mixed by an output projection (out_lin).
  • The total computation stays about the same as one big head, but the model gets many different "views" of the sentence.

3.2 Extract and Plot Real Attention Heads¶

In [11]:
# 'out' and 'sentence' come from Task 2.6 (DistilBERT, output_attentions=True)
attn_tuple = out.attentions
print("Number of tensors in the tuple:", len(attn_tuple))
print("Shape of each tensor (batch, heads, tokens, tokens):", tuple(attn_tuple[0].shape))

tokens = tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(enc["input_ids"][0])
T = len(tokens)
A = torch.stack([a[0] for a in attn_tuple]).numpy()       # (layers=6, heads=12, T, T)
n_layers, n_heads = A.shape[0], A.shape[1]

# ---- measure simple behaviours for all 72 heads ----
prev_share    = np.zeros((n_layers, n_heads))
special_share = np.zeros((n_layers, n_heads))
self_share    = np.zeros((n_layers, n_heads))
it_animal     = np.zeros((n_layers, n_heads))
it_street     = np.zeros((n_layers, n_heads))
head_entropy  = np.zeros((n_layers, n_heads))

i_it, i_animal, i_street = tokens.index("it"), tokens.index("animal"), tokens.index("street")

for l in range(n_layers):
    for h in range(n_heads):
        M = A[l, h]
        prev_share[l, h]    = np.mean([M[i, i - 1] for i in range(1, T)])   # looks at previous token
        special_share[l, h] = M[:, [0, T - 1]].sum(axis=1).mean()           # looks at [CLS]/[SEP]
        self_share[l, h]    = np.mean(np.diag(M))                           # looks at itself
        it_animal[l, h]     = M[i_it, i_animal]                             # 'it' -> 'animal'
        it_street[l, h]     = M[i_it, i_street]                             # 'it' -> 'street'
        head_entropy[l, h]  = entropy(M).mean()                             # how spread out

def pick(score, used):
    # best (layer, head) that was not chosen already
    for idx in np.argsort(score.ravel())[::-1]:
        l, h = divmod(int(idx), n_heads)
        if (l, h) not in used:
            return l, h

choices = [
    ("previous-token head",    prev_share),
    ("attends to [CLS]/[SEP]", special_share),
    ("'it' -> 'animal'",       it_animal),
    ("'it' -> 'street'",       it_street),
    ("looks at itself",        self_share),
    ("most spread out",        head_entropy),
]

used, selected = [], []
for name, score in choices:
    l, h = pick(score, used)
    used.append((l, h))
    selected.append((name, l, h))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(18, 11))
for ax, (name, l, h) in zip(axes.ravel(), selected):
    sns.heatmap(A[l, h], ax=ax, cmap="viridis", cbar=False, xticklabels=tokens, yticklabels=tokens)
    ax.set_title(f"Layer {l} - Head {h}\n({name})", fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlabel("Key (attended token)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Query (current token)")
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
plt.suptitle("Six Real DistilBERT Attention Heads", fontsize=15)
plt.tight_layout()
save_fig("attention_heads.png")
plt.show()

# ---- auto interpretation ----
for name, l, h in selected:
    print(f"Layer {l} Head {h:>2} [{name:24s}] prev-token={prev_share[l,h]:.2f}  "
          f"special={special_share[l,h]:.2f}  self={self_share[l,h]:.2f}  "
          f"it->animal={it_animal[l,h]:.2f}  it->street={it_street[l,h]:.2f}")

Layer 0 Head  1 ['it' -> 'street'        ] prev-token=0.06  special=0.14  self=0.12  it->animal=0.16  it->street=0.21
Layer 1 Head  6 [looks at itself         ] prev-token=0.01  special=0.28  self=0.46  it->animal=0.00  it->street=0.00
Layer 0 Head  0 [most spread out         ] prev-token=0.06  special=0.27  self=0.06  it->animal=0.07  it->street=0.08
  • The output is a tuple of 6 tensors (one per layer), each shaped (batch, 12 heads, tokens, tokens).
  • Different heads show different behaviours on the same sentence. Typical patterns to look for in the grid: a head that attends to the previous token (a bright line just below the diagonal), a head that sends most attention to [CLS]/[SEP], and a head where "it" links to a noun such as "animal" or "street".
  • The title of each plot tells which behaviour the head was selected for; the printed numbers show how strong that behaviour is. This is why many heads are useful: each one learns a different job.

3.3 Head Diversity Measurement¶

In [12]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, layer_id, title in zip(axes, [0, n_layers - 1], ["Layer 0 (early)", f"Layer {n_layers-1} (last)"]):
    ax.bar(range(n_heads), head_entropy[layer_id], color="#66C2A5" if layer_id == 0 else "#FC8D62")
    ax.set_title(f"Average Attention Entropy per Head - {title}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Head number")
    ax.set_xticks(range(n_heads))
axes[0].set_ylabel("Entropy (low = focused, high = spread out)")
plt.tight_layout()
save_fig("attention_entropy.png")
plt.show()

print(f"Mean entropy - layer 0: {head_entropy[0].mean():.3f} | last layer: {head_entropy[-1].mean():.3f}")

Mean entropy - layer 0: 1.686 | last layer: 2.010
  • Low entropy means a head is focused on few tokens; high entropy means it spreads its attention widely.
  • The heads inside the same layer have different entropies, so they do not all behave alike. Compare the two printed layer averages to see whether early or late layers are more spread out — this is one sentence only, so keep conclusions modest.

3.4 Sinusoidal Positional Encoding from Scratch¶

In [13]:
def sinusoidal_pe(n_positions, d_model):
    pe = np.zeros((n_positions, d_model))
    pos = np.arange(n_positions)[:, None]                    # positions 0..49
    two_i = np.arange(0, d_model, 2)[None, :]                # 0, 2, 4, ...
    angle = pos / np.power(10000, two_i / d_model)
    pe[:, 0::2] = np.sin(angle)                              # even dimensions
    pe[:, 1::2] = np.cos(angle)                              # odd dimensions
    return pe

PE = sinusoidal_pe(50, 128)
print("PE shape:", PE.shape)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
sns.heatmap(PE, cmap="coolwarm", center=0)
plt.title("Sinusoidal Positional Encoding (50 positions x 128 dimensions)")
plt.xlabel("Dimension")
plt.ylabel("Position")
save_fig("positional_encoding.png")
plt.show()

PE shape: (50, 128)
  • Each position gets a unique pattern of sines and cosines.
  • Low dimensions (left) change fast (high frequency) and high dimensions (right) change slowly (low frequency) — like the digits of a clock, so every position has its own "fingerprint".
  • Because sin/cos of shifted angles are linear combinations of each other, relative offsets (position + k) are easy for the model to learn.

3.5 Position Makes Identical Words Different¶

In [14]:
def cosine(u, v):
    return float(u @ v / (np.linalg.norm(u) * np.linalg.norm(v)))

word_vec = rng.normal(size=128)                    # one word embedding

with_pe_3  = word_vec + PE[3]                      # same word at position 3
with_pe_20 = word_vec + PE[20]                     # same word at position 20

print("Cosine similarity WITHOUT PE :", round(cosine(word_vec, word_vec), 4))
print("Cosine similarity WITH PE    :", round(cosine(with_pe_3, with_pe_20), 4))

Cosine similarity WITHOUT PE : 1.0
Cosine similarity WITH PE    : 0.8657
  • Without positional encoding the same word has identical vectors everywhere (similarity = 1.0).
  • After adding PE, the word at position 3 and position 20 becomes different (similarity below 1).
  • Combined with Task 2.5: attention alone cannot tell positions apart, but once PE is added to the embeddings, the same word at different places produces different Q, K, V — so order information is no longer lost.

3.6 Learned Positional Embeddings in a Real Model¶

In [15]:
pos_weights = distil.distilbert.embeddings.position_embeddings.weight.detach().numpy()
print("Position embedding table shape:", pos_weights.shape)

first64 = pos_weights[:64]
normed = first64 / np.linalg.norm(first64, axis=1, keepdims=True)
sim_matrix = normed @ normed.T                    # cosine similarity (64 x 64)

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 6))
sns.heatmap(sim_matrix, cmap="viridis")
plt.title("Cosine Similarity of Learned Position Embeddings (first 64 positions)")
plt.xlabel("Position")
plt.ylabel("Position")
save_fig("learned_positions.png")
plt.show()

Position embedding table shape: (512, 768)
  • BERT-style models learn one vector per position (a 512 × 768 table) instead of using fixed sine/cosine formulas.
  • The heatmap shows how similar positions are to each other — neighbouring positions are usually more similar than far-away ones if the model learned a smooth position pattern.
  • The table has only 512 rows, so the model has no vector for position 513 — this is the origin of the 512-token context-length limit.
  • (T5 uses relative position biases instead; we meet it in Task 5.)

3.7 Layer Normalization from Scratch¶

In [16]:
def layer_norm(x, gamma=1.0, beta=0.0, eps=1e-5):
    mean = x.mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True)              # over FEATURES of each token
    var  = x.var(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return gamma * (x - mean) / np.sqrt(var + eps) + beta

tokens_x = rng.normal(size=(4, 8)) * 5 + 3             # 4 tokens, 8 features (not normalised on purpose)
my_ln = layer_norm(tokens_x)

print("Per-token mean:", my_ln.mean(axis=1).round(6))
print("Per-token std :", my_ln.std(axis=1).round(4))

torch_ln = torch.nn.LayerNorm(8)(torch.tensor(tokens_x, dtype=torch.float32)).detach().numpy()
print("\nMatches torch.nn.LayerNorm(8)?", np.allclose(my_ln, torch_ln, atol=1e-5))

Per-token mean: [ 0. -0. -0.  0.]
Per-token std : [1. 1. 1. 1.]

Matches torch.nn.LayerNorm(8)? True
  • For each token separately, LayerNorm subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation over its features → mean ≈ 0 and std ≈ 1.
  • gamma (scale) and beta (shift) then let the model re-adjust the values if it wants.
  • Our function matches torch.nn.LayerNorm (True).

3.8 LayerNorm vs BatchNorm¶

In [17]:
# BatchNorm: normalise each FEATURE across the 4 tokens (over the batch dimension)
bn = (tokens_x - tokens_x.mean(axis=0)) / np.sqrt(tokens_x.var(axis=0) + 1e-5)

print("BatchNorm - per-FEATURE mean:", bn.mean(axis=0).round(4))
print("BatchNorm - per-TOKEN   mean:", bn.mean(axis=1).round(4), "<- NOT normalised")
print("LayerNorm - per-TOKEN   mean:", my_ln.mean(axis=1).round(4), "<- normalised")

# LayerNorm weights of DistilBERT's embedding layer
emb_ln = distil.distilbert.embeddings.LayerNorm
print("\nEmbedding LayerNorm weight (gamma) shape:", tuple(emb_ln.weight.shape))
print("Embedding LayerNorm bias   (beta)  shape:", tuple(emb_ln.bias.shape))
print("First 5 gamma values:", emb_ln.weight[:5].detach().numpy().round(3))
print("First 5 beta values :", emb_ln.bias[:5].detach().numpy().round(3))

BatchNorm - per-FEATURE mean: [ 0.  0.  0. -0.  0. -0. -0. -0.]
BatchNorm - per-TOKEN   mean: [-0.2741  0.4353 -0.3009  0.1397] <- NOT normalised
LayerNorm - per-TOKEN   mean: [ 0. -0. -0.  0.] <- normalised

Embedding LayerNorm weight (gamma) shape: (768,)
Embedding LayerNorm bias   (beta)  shape: (768,)
First 5 gamma values: [0.845 0.797 0.733 0.759 0.801]
First 5 beta values : [ 0.044  0.061  0.069  0.087 -0.058]
Point LayerNorm BatchNorm
What is normalised over The features of one token One feature across the batch
Depends on batch size? No Yes (poor with small batches)
Variable-length sequences / padding Works — each token is independent Padding tokens distort the batch statistics
Train vs test behaviour Same Needs running averages at test time
Used in Transformers CNNs (and the ANN in PR 2)
  • Transformers use LayerNorm because sentence lengths and padding change from batch to batch, and LayerNorm does not depend on other sentences.
  • In DistilBERT, gamma is a learned scale vector (768 values) and beta a learned shift vector (768 values), one pair per feature.

Task 4: Transformer Encoder Architecture & Masked Self-Attention¶

4.1 Encoder Architecture¶

Input embeddings + positional information
        ↓
  [ Encoder block ] × N  (DistilBERT: N = 6)
     1. Multi-head self-attention
     2. Add (residual connection) + Layer Norm
     3. Position-wise feed-forward network  (expand 768 → 3072, non-linearity, project back to 768)
     4. Add (residual connection) + Layer Norm
        ↓
  Output: one contextual vector per token
  • Each of the 6 layers of DistilBERT contains exactly this block: self-attention, add & norm, feed-forward, add & norm.
  • "Encoder" means every token can see every other token in both directions (left and right).

4.2 Print and Read the Real Encoder¶

In [18]:
print(distil.distilbert)

print("\nModules inside ONE encoder layer (layer 0):")
for name, module in distil.distilbert.transformer.layer[0].named_modules():
    if name:
        print(f"  {name:25s} -> {module.__class__.__name__}")

DistilBertModel(
  (embeddings): Embeddings(
    (word_embeddings): Embedding(30522, 768, padding_idx=0)
    (position_embeddings): Embedding(512, 768)
    (LayerNorm): LayerNorm((768,), eps=1e-12, elementwise_affine=True, bias=True)
    (dropout): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
  )
  (transformer): Transformer(
    (layer): ModuleList(
      (0-5): 6 x TransformerBlock(
        (attention): MultiHeadSelfAttention(
          (dropout): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
          (q_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
          (k_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
          (v_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
          (out_lin): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=768, bias=True)
        )
        (sa_layer_norm): LayerNorm((768,), eps=1e-12, elementwise_affine=True, bias=True)
        (ffn): FFN(
          (dropout): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
          (lin1): Linear(in_features=768, out_features=3072, bias=True)
          (lin2): Linear(in_features=3072, out_features=768, bias=True)
          (activation): GELUActivation()
        )
        (output_layer_norm): LayerNorm((768,), eps=1e-12, elementwise_affine=True, bias=True)
      )
    )
  )
)

Modules inside ONE encoder layer (layer 0):
  attention                 -> MultiHeadSelfAttention
  attention.dropout         -> Dropout
  attention.q_lin           -> Linear
  attention.k_lin           -> Linear
  attention.v_lin           -> Linear
  attention.out_lin         -> Linear
  sa_layer_norm             -> LayerNorm
  ffn                       -> FFN
  ffn.dropout               -> Dropout
  ffn.lin1                  -> Linear
  ffn.lin2                  -> Linear
  ffn.activation            -> GELUActivation
  output_layer_norm         -> LayerNorm
Component Module name in DistilBERT
Token embedding distilbert.embeddings.word_embeddings
Position embedding distilbert.embeddings.position_embeddings
Embedding LayerNorm distilbert.embeddings.LayerNorm
Attention block attention → q_lin, k_lin, v_lin, out_lin
Layer norm after attention sa_layer_norm
Feed-forward block ffn → lin1 (768 → 3072), activation (GELU), lin2 (3072 → 768)
Layer norm after feed-forward output_layer_norm
  • Every layer has two layer norms (sa_layer_norm and output_layer_norm).
  • The feed-forward network expands 768 → 3072 and projects back to 768.

4.3 Where Do the Parameters Live?¶

In [19]:
groups = {"Embeddings": 0, "Attention": 0, "Feed-forward": 0, "Layer norms": 0, "Classification head": 0}

for name, p in distil.named_parameters():
    n = p.numel()
    if "layer_norm" in name or "LayerNorm" in name:
        groups["Layer norms"] += n
    elif "embeddings" in name:
        groups["Embeddings"] += n
    elif "attention" in name:
        groups["Attention"] += n
    elif "ffn" in name:
        groups["Feed-forward"] += n
    else:
        groups["Classification head"] += n

param_df = pd.DataFrame({"Component": list(groups.keys()), "Parameters": list(groups.values())})
param_df["Share (%)"] = (param_df["Parameters"] / param_df["Parameters"].sum() * 100).round(2)
display(param_df)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax = sns.barplot(x="Component", y="Parameters", data=param_df, palette="Set2")
for i, row in param_df.iterrows():
    ax.text(i, row["Parameters"], f"{row['Share (%)']}%", ha="center", va="bottom")

plt.ylabel("Number of parameters")

Component Parameters Share (%)
0 Embeddings 23834112 35.60
1 Attention 14174208 21.17
2 Feed-forward 28334592 42.32
3 Layer norms 19968 0.03
4 Classification head 592130 0.88 
Largest component: Feed-forward
  • The feed-forward blocks and the embedding tables hold most of the parameters; attention and layer norms hold a much smaller share.
  • This suggests that the model stores much of its knowledge in the feed-forward layers (large "memory" matrices) and in the word embeddings, while attention mainly decides where to look.

4.4 Use the Encoder: Fill-Mask¶

In [20]:
fill = pipeline("fill-mask", model=DISTIL_BASE)

mask_sentences = [
    "The capital of France is [MASK].",
    "I went to the [MASK] to buy some bread.",
    "She opened the [MASK] and started to read.",
]

rows = []
for s in mask_sentences:
    for r in fill(s, top_k=3):
        rows.append({"Sentence": s, "Prediction": r["token_str"], "Score": round(r["score"], 4)})
display(pd.DataFrame(rows))
Sentence Prediction Score
0 The capital of France is [MASK]. marseille 0.1427
1 The capital of France is [MASK]. nantes 0.0902
2 The capital of France is [MASK]. toulouse 0.0881
3 I went to the [MASK] to buy some bread. bakery 0.2565
4 I went to the [MASK] to buy some bread. market 0.1430
5 I went to the [MASK] to buy some bread. kitchen 0.0992
6 She opened the [MASK] and started to read. door 0.2403
7 She opened the [MASK] and started to read. book 0.2080
8 She opened the [MASK] and started to read. notebook 0.0833
  • The model fills the blank using words on both sides of [MASK] (for example "capital of France" on the left and the full stop on the right).
  • This is the bidirectional behaviour of an encoder, and it is how BERT-style models are pre-trained.

4.5 Bidirectional Attention Heatmap¶

In [21]:
# Last-layer attention averaged over the 12 heads (same sentence as Task 2.6)
bi_attn = out.attentions[-1][0].mean(dim=0).numpy()

upper = np.triu(bi_attn, k=1).sum() / bi_attn.sum()
lower = np.tril(bi_attn, k=-1).sum() / bi_attn.sum()
print(f"Share of attention ABOVE the diagonal (future tokens): {upper:.2f}")
print(f"Share of attention BELOW the diagonal (past tokens)  : {lower:.2f}")

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.heatmap(bi_attn, cmap="viridis", xticklabels=tokens, yticklabels=tokens)
plt.title("DistilBERT (Encoder) - Last Layer Attention, averaged over heads")
plt.xlabel("Key (attended token)")
plt.ylabel("Query (current token)")
plt.show()

Share of attention ABOVE the diagonal (future tokens): 0.57
Share of attention BELOW the diagonal (past tokens)  : 0.28
  • There are non-zero weights both above and below the diagonal — every token looks at tokens to its left and right.
  • This is perfect for understanding a full sentence, but it is not allowed in a language model that must predict the next word: it would simply "see the answer". That is why the decoder needs masked self-attention.

4.6 Masked (Causal) Self-Attention from Scratch¶

In [22]:
n_tok = 6
Xc = rng.normal(size=(n_tok, 8))
Qc, Kc, Vc = Xc @ Wq, Xc @ Wk, Xc @ Wv

# -infinity ABOVE the diagonal, 0 on and below it
causal_mask = np.triu(np.full((n_tok, n_tok), -np.inf), k=1)
print("Causal mask:\n", causal_mask)

_, causal_weights, _ = scaled_dot_product_attention(Qc, Kc, Vc, mask=causal_mask)

print("\nUpper triangle is zero ?", np.triu(causal_weights, k=1).max() == 0)
print("Row sums:", causal_weights.sum(axis=1).round(6))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))
sns.heatmap(np.isinf(causal_mask).astype(int), ax=axes[0], cmap="Reds", cbar=False, annot=True)
axes[0].set_title("Causal Mask (1 = blocked, -inf)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Key position"); axes[0].set_ylabel("Query position")
sns.heatmap(causal_weights, ax=axes[1], cmap="viridis", annot=True, fmt=".2f")
axes[1].set_title("Attention After Causal Mask")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Key position"); axes[1].set_ylabel("Query position")
plt.tight_layout()
save_fig("causal_mask.png")
plt.show()

Causal mask:
 [[  0. -inf -inf -inf -inf -inf]
 [  0.   0. -inf -inf -inf -inf]
 [  0.   0.   0. -inf -inf -inf]
 [  0.   0.   0.   0. -inf -inf]
 [  0.   0.   0.   0.   0. -inf]
 [  0.   0.   0.   0.   0.   0.]]

Upper triangle is zero ? True
Row sums: [1. 1. 1. 1. 1. 1.]
  • The attention matrix is now lower-triangular: token i can only look at tokens 0 … i (itself and the past).
  • Rows still sum to 1, because softmax is applied after the mask.
  • We add −∞ before softmax (so e^(−∞) = 0 and the remaining weights are renormalised to sum to 1). If we simply zeroed the weights afterwards, the rows would no longer sum to 1 and the future tokens would still have influenced the softmax.

4.7 Causal Mask in a Real Decoder (GPT-2)¶

In [23]:
gpt_tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(GPT2_ID)
gpt2 = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(GPT2_ID, attn_implementation="eager")
gpt2.eval()

enc_g = gpt_tok(sentence, return_tensors="pt")
with torch.no_grad():
    out_g = gpt2(**enc_g, output_attentions=True)

attn_g = out_g.attentions[-1][0, 0].numpy()                  # last layer, head 0
gpt_tokens = [t.replace("Ġ", "") for t in gpt_tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(enc_g["input_ids"][0])]

upper_max = np.triu(attn_g, k=1).max()
print("Largest value above the diagonal:", upper_max)
print("Everything above the diagonal is (almost) zero ?", upper_max < 1e-6)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 6))
sns.heatmap(bi_attn, ax=axes[0], cmap="viridis", xticklabels=tokens, yticklabels=tokens)
axes[0].set_title("DistilBERT - bidirectional (avg over heads)")
sns.heatmap(attn_g, ax=axes[1], cmap="viridis", xticklabels=gpt_tokens, yticklabels=gpt_tokens)
axes[1].set_title("GPT-2 - causal (last layer, head 0)")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("Key (attended token)"); ax.set_ylabel("Query (current token)")
plt.tight_layout()
save_fig("bidirectional_vs_causal.png")
plt.show()

Largest value above the diagonal: 0.0
Everything above the diagonal is (almost) zero ? True
  • The GPT-2 heatmap is a perfect lower triangle: the numeric check (np.triu(attn, k=1).max() < 1e-6) confirms that no token attends to the future.
  • Compared with DistilBERT (full square), GPT-2 can only use left context — that is what makes text generation possible.

4.8 Padding Mask vs Causal Mask¶

In [24]:
pad_batch = tok(
    ["I love it.", "This movie was long, slow and honestly a little boring."],
    padding=True, return_tensors="pt"
)
with torch.no_grad():
    out_p = distil(**pad_batch, output_attentions=True)

mask = pad_batch["attention_mask"]
for b in range(2):
    pad_pos = (mask[b] == 0).nonzero().flatten()
    if len(pad_pos) == 0:
        print(f"Sentence {b}: no padding")
        continue
    # attention received by padding columns, across ALL layers and heads
    received = max(layer_attn[b][:, :, pad_pos].max().item() for layer_attn in out_p.attentions)
    print(f"Sentence {b}: {len(pad_pos)} padding positions -> maximum attention they receive = {received:.2e}")

Sentence 0: 8 padding positions -> maximum attention they receive = 0.00e+00
Sentence 1: no padding
Point Padding mask Causal mask
Purpose Ignore [PAD] tokens added to make batch lengths equal Stop a token from seeing future tokens
Shape / pattern Columns of padded positions are blocked Upper triangle is blocked
Depends on The sentence lengths in the batch Only the sequence length
Model families Used by all (encoder, decoder, encoder-decoder) Decoder models (GPT-2, decoder of T5)
  • The padding positions receive (almost) zero attention, so padding does not change the result for the real tokens.

Task 5: Cross-Attention, Decoder Architecture & Inference¶

5.1 Decoder Architecture¶

The original Transformer decoder block has three sub-layers:

Masked multi-head self-attention  →  Add & Norm
Cross-attention over the ENCODER output  →  Add & Norm
Feed-forward network  →  Add & Norm
        ↓  (after the last block)
Linear layer  →  Softmax over the vocabulary  →  next-token probabilities

Three Transformer families:

Family Example Blocks used
Encoder-only BERT, DistilBERT Encoder only (bidirectional) — understanding tasks
Decoder-only GPT-2 Decoder without cross-attention (causal) — text generation
Encoder-decoder T5 Encoder + decoder with cross-attention — translation, summarisation

5.2 Cross-Attention¶

In cross-attention, the Queries come from the DECODER, while the Keys and Values come from the ENCODER output.

  • It lets the decoder look at the source sentence while writing each word of the target sentence (for example, while writing "maison" it can look at "house").
  • It is the Transformer version of Luong attention (Task 2.4): decoder state = query, encoder states = keys/values — only now it uses Q/K/V projections and runs in parallel without RNNs.

5.3 Run an Encoder-Decoder Model (T5-small)¶

In [25]:
t5_tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(T5_ID)
t5 = T5ForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(T5_ID, attn_implementation="eager")
t5.eval()

# Newer transformers versions (v5) removed the translation/summarisation pipelines,
# so we try the pipeline first and fall back to model.generate().
try:
    translator = pipeline("translation_en_to_fr", model=T5_ID)
    summarizer = pipeline("summarization", model=T5_ID)
    print("Using Hugging Face pipelines")
except Exception:
    translator = summarizer = None
    print("Pipelines not available in this version -> using t5.generate() directly")

def t5_generate(prefix, text, **gen_kwargs):
    inputs = t5_tok(prefix + text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=512)
    with torch.no_grad():
        ids = t5.generate(**inputs, **gen_kwargs)
    return t5_tok.decode(ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

def translate_fr(text):
    if translator is not None:
        return translator(text)[0]["translation_text"]
    return t5_generate("translate English to French: ", text, max_new_tokens=100, num_beams=4)

def summarize(text, max_length=60, min_length=20):
    if summarizer is not None:
        return summarizer(text, max_length=max_length, min_length=min_length)[0]["summary_text"]
    return t5_generate("summarize: ", text, max_length=max_length, min_length=min_length,
                       num_beams=4, early_stopping=True)

# ---- Translation of 3 sentences ----
en_sentences = [
    "The house is small and very old.",
    "I would like a cup of coffee, please.",
    "Machine learning is changing the world.",
]
display(pd.DataFrame({"English": en_sentences, "French (t5-small)": [translate_fr(s) for s in en_sentences]}))

# ---- Summarisation of one paragraph (replace with any real article you like) ----
news_text = (
    "India's Chandrayaan-3 spacecraft made a soft landing near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023, "
    "making India the fourth country to land on the Moon and the first to touch down so close to the lunar south pole. "
    "The lander, called Vikram, carried a small rover named Pragyan that drove out onto the surface to study the soil "
    "and measure its temperature. Scientists at the Indian Space Research Organisation said the mission cost much less "
    "than many comparable missions, and they praised the team for careful design and testing. Engineers had spent years "
    "improving the landing system after the previous attempt, Chandrayaan-2, failed in 2019 when its lander crashed "
    "during the final descent. The success was celebrated across the country, and the landing site was later named "
    "Shiv Shakti Point. The mission lasted about two weeks, which is the length of one lunar day, after which the lander "
    "and rover were put into sleep mode as the lunar night began."
)
summary = summarize(news_text, max_length=60, min_length=20)
print("Input length  :", len(news_text.split()), "words")
print("Summary length:", len(summary.split()), "words")
print("Summary       :", summary)

Using Hugging Face pipelines
English French (t5-small)
0 The house is small and very old. La maison est petite et très ancienne.
1 I would like a cup of coffee, please. Je voudrais une tasse de café, je vous prie.
2 Machine learning is changing the world. L'apprentissage des machines change le monde. 
Input length  : 161 words
Summary length: 54 words
Summary       : Chandrayaan-3 made a soft landing near the moon's south pole on 23 august 2023 . the lander carried a small rover named Pragyan that drove out onto the surface to study the soil and measure its temperature . engineers had spent years improving the landing system after the previous attempt failed in 2019 .
  • T5 is a text-to-text model: the task is selected with a text prefix ("translate English to French: ", "summarize: ").
  • It uses both an encoder (reads the English text) and a decoder (writes French / the summary), connected by cross-attention.
  • t5-small is a very small model, so expect imperfect French and a summary that may copy phrases from the input.

5.4 Extract and Plot Cross-Attention¶

In [26]:
src_text = "translate English to French: The house is small."
tgt_text = "La maison est petite."

src = t5_tok(src_text, return_tensors="pt")
labels = t5_tok(tgt_text, return_tensors="pt").input_ids

with torch.no_grad():
    out_t5 = t5(input_ids=src.input_ids, labels=labels, output_attentions=True)

# cross_attentions: one tensor per decoder layer, each (batch, heads=8, target_tokens, source_tokens)
cross = out_t5.cross_attentions[-1][0].mean(dim=0).numpy()     # last decoder layer, averaged over 8 heads

src_tokens = t5_tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(src.input_ids[0])
tgt_tokens = t5_tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(labels[0])
print("Cross-attention shape (output tokens x input tokens):", cross.shape)

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
sns.heatmap(cross, cmap="viridis", xticklabels=src_tokens, yticklabels=tgt_tokens, annot=True, fmt=".2f")
plt.title("T5-small Cross-Attention (last decoder layer, averaged over 8 heads)")
plt.xlabel("Input tokens (encoder)")
plt.ylabel("Output tokens (decoder)")
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
save_fig("cross_attention.png")
plt.show()

for i, t in enumerate(tgt_tokens):
    j = cross[i].argmax()
    print(f"Output token {t:>10s}  ->  most attended input token: {src_tokens[j]:>10s} ({cross[i, j]:.2f})")

Cross-attention shape (output tokens x input tokens): (6, 11)

Output token        ▁La  ->  most attended input token:          : (0.16)
Output token    ▁maison  ->  most attended input token:          : (0.32)
Output token       ▁est  ->  most attended input token:          : (0.19)

Output token          .  ->  most attended input token:    ▁French (0.19)

  • Each row is one output (French) token and each column is one input (English) token; bright cells show where the decoder looked while writing that word.
  • Check the printed alignment: does "maison" attend to "house", and "petite" to "small"? A sensible alignment is a sign that cross-attention is doing the "look at the source" job.
  • Averaging over heads and using only the last layer can blur the picture, and attention often goes to the end-of-sentence token </s> as well — so the alignment is usually partly sensible, not perfect.

5.5 Inference Is Autoregressive: Manual Greedy Loop¶

In [27]:
prompt = "Artificial intelligence will"
enc_p = gpt_tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt")
ids = enc_p["input_ids"]

# Our own greedy loop: predict ONE token, append it, repeat
for step in range(20):
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = gpt2(ids).logits                      # (1, length, vocab)
    next_id = logits[:, -1, :].argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    ids = torch.cat([ids, next_id], dim=1)

manual_text = gpt_tok.decode(ids[0])

# The library way
with torch.no_grad():
    gen_ids = gpt2.generate(**enc_p, max_new_tokens=20, do_sample=False, pad_token_id=gpt_tok.eos_token_id)
generate_text = gpt_tok.decode(gen_ids[0])

print("Manual loop :", manual_text)
print("generate()  :", generate_text)
print("\nIdentical ?", torch.equal(ids, gen_ids))

Manual loop : Artificial intelligence will be able to do things like search for and find people, and to do things like find out who
generate()  : Artificial intelligence will be able to do things like search for and find people, and to do things like find out who

Identical ? True
  • A decoder generates ONE token at a time: it predicts the next token from the last position's logits, appends it to the input, and runs again.
  • Our simple loop gives the identical output to model.generate(do_sample=False) — generate() is just this loop with extra features.

5.6 Decoding Strategies¶

In [28]:
def decode(strategy, seed=None, **kwargs):
    if seed is not None:
        torch.manual_seed(seed)
    with torch.no_grad():
        g = gpt2.generate(**enc_p, max_new_tokens=40, pad_token_id=gpt_tok.eos_token_id, **kwargs)
    new_tokens = g[0][enc_p["input_ids"].shape[1]:]
    text = gpt_tok.decode(g[0], skip_special_tokens=True).replace("\n", " ")
    unique_ratio = len(set(new_tokens.tolist())) / len(new_tokens)      # low = repetitive
    return {"Strategy": strategy, "Seed": seed, "Unique-token ratio": round(unique_ratio, 2), "Output": text}

runs = [
    decode("(a) Greedy", do_sample=False),
    decode("(b) Beam search (5 beams)", num_beams=5, early_stopping=True, do_sample=False),
    decode("(c) Temperature 0.7", seed=1, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7, top_k=0),
    decode("(c) Temperature 0.7", seed=2, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7, top_k=0),
    decode("(d) Temperature 1.5", seed=1, do_sample=True, temperature=1.5, top_k=0),
    decode("(d) Temperature 1.5", seed=2, do_sample=True, temperature=1.5, top_k=0),
    decode("(e) top_k=50 + top_p=0.9", seed=1, do_sample=True, top_k=50, top_p=0.9),
]

pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", None)
display(pd.DataFrame(runs))

1 (b) Beam search (5 beams) NaN 0.65 Artificial intelligence will be the next big thing, and it's going to take a lot of work to get there. "I think it's going to take a lot of work to get there," he said

3 (c) Temperature 0.7 2.0 0.78 Artificial intelligence will not be able to solve problems that have never been solved. The researchers note that the story of the self-driving car is like a tale of two halves: one is a self-driving
4 (d) Temperature 1.5 1.0 1.00 Artificial intelligence will upset inertia in difficult news ones. Countries humans would respect assimil c about every trial, scaven- Detection organizations from the above won % of dislressed orally Fastaturation rofter going judge sentenced k move Tid
5 (d) Temperature 1.5 2.0 1.00 Artificial intelligence will not similarly distress down that angry increase paradigm and presume elsear characterShell pervasive strandsUpon childinitiality gradient spweet votingIn acid GUI libraries pigples are choosing SpecificesKennlaus communities values inputnow

  • Greedy and beam search are deterministic: same prompt → same output, and they tend to become repetitive.
  • Temperature rescales the probabilities: 0.7 (sharper) → safer, more predictable text; 1.5 (flatter) → more random and often less coherent. Sampling runs with different seeds give different outputs.
  • top-k keeps only the k most likely tokens and top-p keeps the smallest set whose probability adds to p — both cut off very unlikely words, giving a good balance of variety and sense.

5.7 KV-Cache Speed-Up¶

In [29]:
def time_generation(use_cache, runs=3, new_tokens=100):
    times = []
    for _ in range(runs):
        start = time.time()
        with torch.no_grad():
            gpt2.generate(**enc_p, max_new_tokens=new_tokens, min_new_tokens=new_tokens,
                          do_sample=False, use_cache=use_cache, pad_token_id=gpt_tok.eos_token_id)
        times.append(time.time() - start)
    return np.mean(times)

_ = time_generation(True, runs=1, new_tokens=10)      # warm-up

t_cache    = time_generation(True)
t_no_cache = time_generation(False)

print(f"use_cache=True  : {t_cache:.2f} s (average of 3 runs)")
print(f"use_cache=False : {t_no_cache:.2f} s (average of 3 runs)")
print(f"Speed-up        : {t_no_cache / t_cache:.1f}x")

use_cache=True  : 12.42 s (average of 3 runs)
use_cache=False : 60.66 s (average of 3 runs)
Speed-up        : 4.9x
  • The Keys and Values of earlier tokens never change, so they can be stored (cached) instead of recomputed at every step.
  • With the cache, each new step processes only the newest token; without it, the whole sequence is processed again and again.
  • The printed speed-up is the main speed trick of Transformer inference.

def evaluate(max_len):
    start = time.time()
    raw = clf(texts, truncation=True, max_length=max_len, batch_size=16)
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    preds = [1 if r["label"] == "POSITIVE" else 0 for r in raw]

6.3 Cost Grows with Sequence Length¶

In [34]:

    assert inp["input_ids"].shape[1] == L
    with torch.no_grad():

        start = time.time()

        fwd_times.append((time.time() - start) / 10)

Time(512) / Time(32) = 7.6x  while length grew 16x
Fitted growth exponent = 0.77  (1.0 = linear, 2.0 = quadratic)
  • Attention compares every token with every other token, so the attention cost grows roughly with the square of the length — this is the reason for the 512-token limit.
  • Be honest about the measurement: on a small CPU with short sequences, the linear parts (feed-forward layers, projections) dominate, so the measured curve usually looks closer to linear than quadratic. The exponent printed above tells which one you really saw; the quadratic term only takes over at much longer lengths.

6.5 Build the Mini Application: text_toolkit()¶

In [36]:
def text_toolkit(text):
    # Returns sentiment, summary and French translation of the summary
    result = {"sentiment": None, "score": None, "summary": None, "french": None, "note": ""}

    # ---- handle bad input ----
    if text is None or not str(text).strip():
        result["note"] = "Empty input - please provide some text."
        return result
    text = str(text).strip()

    # ---- (a) sentiment (DistilBERT) - long text is truncated to 512 tokens ----
    n_tokens = len(tok(text)["input_ids"])
    s = clf(text, truncation=True, max_length=512)[0]
    result["sentiment"], result["score"] = s["label"], round(s["score"], 4)
    if n_tokens > 512:
        result["note"] += f"Input has {n_tokens} tokens; only the first 512 were used. "

    # ---- (b) summary (T5-small, max_length = 60) ----
    if len(text.split()) < 15:
        result["summary"] = text
        result["note"] += "Text too short to summarise; original used. "
    else:
        result["summary"] = summarize(text, max_length=60, min_length=20)

    # ---- (c) French translation of the summary ----
    result["french"] = translate_fr(result["summary"])
    return result

passages = {
    "Movie review": (
        "I went into this film with low expectations and was pleasantly surprised. The story is simple, "
        "but the acting is warm and funny, and the final twenty minutes had the whole audience clapping. "
        "A few jokes fall flat, yet the film never stops being charming. I would happily watch it again."
    ),
    "News paragraph": news_text,
    "My own passage": (   # <- replace with your own passage
        "This semester I started learning how Transformers work. At first the idea of attention felt confusing, "
        "but after rebuilding it in NumPy and comparing it with a real model, it finally made sense. "
        "I am proud that I can now explain why queries, keys and values are needed."
    ),
}

rows = []
for name, passage in passages.items():
    r = text_toolkit(passage)
    rows.append({"Passage": name, "Sentiment": r["sentiment"], "Score": r["score"],
                 "Summary": r["summary"], "French": r["french"], "Note": r["note"]})

# Edge cases: empty input and a very long input
for name, passage in [("Empty text", ""), ("Very long text", news_text * 20)]:
    r = text_toolkit(passage)
    rows.append({"Passage": name, "Sentiment": r["sentiment"], "Score": r["score"],
                 "Summary": r["summary"], "French": r["french"], "Note": r["note"]})

pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 120)
display(pd.DataFrame(rows))

Task 6.6 - What I Learned About Transformers¶

1. What I understand best¶

I now understand Self-Attention, Multi-Head Attention, and Positional Encoding. These concepts explain how Transformers process text efficiently.

2. What is still unclear¶

The internal optimization of very large Transformer models and advanced attention mechanisms still require more practice.

3. What matched the theory¶

The manually implemented attention mechanism produced results similar to the real DistilBERT model, confirming that the theory of scaled dot-product attention is correct.

4. What surprised me¶

I was surprised that Transformers process all tokens in parallel while still learning relationships between distant words.

5. Two disadvantages observed¶

  • Transformer models require high computation and memory, especially for long sequences.
  • Attention computation becomes expensive as the sequence length increases.

6. Real-world application¶

I would build an AI Recipe Recommendation Assistant that identifies ingredients from a refrigerator image and suggests recipes. This application would use a Vision Transformer (ViT) for image understanding and a Large Language Model (LLM) for generating recipe recommendations.

        round(t_no_cache / t_cache, 1), int((halluc_df["Grade"] == "Correct").sum()),
    ],
})
display(summary_numbers)
